text: Over fifteen thousand active satellites now crowd low Earth orbit — sharing it with the debris of every collision that came before.
And every day, operators get the same kind of warning: something is about to pass dangerously close. Act — and burn precious fuel. Or wait… and hope the next update brings better news.

We started with real data — over thirteen thousand warning sequences from the European Space Agency. And here's the honest part. When E.S.A. ran this as a challenge, only twelve of ninety-seven teams beat the simplest rule there is: just trust the latest warning.

So we didn't fight that rule. We built on it. Our decision layer learns when to act, when to wait, and when to simply keep watching — and it tells you why. On events it has never seen, it beats the baseline.

When a dodge is needed, we test every option. For an upcoming close approach to the Space Station, we screened a hundred and forty-four burns against nearly seven thousand objects. Two of them look almost identical — twenty-two kilometres of clearance. But one quietly steers into a brand-new close call. We pick the one that doesn't.

And if a collision did happen? We simulate the debris cloud with NASA's breakup model. Eleven thousand fragments, spreading around the planet within days. Nearly nine thousand satellites would face new close passes.
That changes the question. Two warnings with the same probability are not equally dangerous. Ranking by expected harm reshuffles more than half of them.

We map the objects that spread the most risk — and IBM's Granite model writes the operator brief. Every number in it is checked against our analysis. If the model invents one, we throw the brief away.

All of this runs on IBM LinuxONE — a z seventeen, with the Telum two processor. Same code, same results, on a big-endian architecture. It ships as a container on IBM's own image, Granite runs right on the machine — so sensitive orbit data never leaves it — and every recommendation lands in a tamper-evident audit log.
Probability tells you how likely. We tell you what it would cost — and which dodge doesn't start a cascade.
